questions.stem: The RBA raises the cash rate. What does the diagram show happening?
options: Demand shifts left: price falls, quantity falls
Demand shifts right: price rises, quantity rises
Supply shifts left
Neither curve moves
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates make borrowing dearer, so fewer people can afford to buy. Demand shifts left and both price and quantity fall.

questions.stem: After the RBA raises the cash rate, who bears the effect shown?
options: Both buyers and sellers, since price and quantity both change
Only buyers, because the price changed
Only sellers, because they set the price
Nobody, because the market returns to the old point
questions.explanation: The new crossing point sits at a different price *and* a different quantity, so both sides are affected. Reading only the price change is the commonest mistake with these diagrams.

questions.stem: The RBA cuts the cash rate. What does the diagram show happening?
options: Neither curve moves
Demand shifts right: price rises, quantity rises
Demand shifts left: price falls, quantity falls
Supply shifts right
questions.explanation: Cheaper borrowing brings more buyers into the market at every price, so demand shifts right and both price and quantity rise.

questions.stem: After the RBA cuts the cash rate, who bears the effect shown?
options: Nobody, because the market returns to the old point
Both buyers and sellers, since price and quantity both change
Only buyers, because the price changed
Only sellers, because they set the price
questions.explanation: The new crossing point sits at a different price *and* a different quantity, so both sides are affected. Reading only the price change is the commonest mistake with these diagrams.

questions.stem: The government subsidises solar panels. What does the diagram show happening?
options: Demand shifts right
Neither curve moves
Supply shifts right: price falls, quantity rises
Supply shifts left: price rises, quantity falls
questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers the cost of producing each panel, so more is supplied at every price. Supply shifts right, price falls and quantity rises.

questions.stem: After the government subsidises solar panels, who bears the effect shown?
options: Both buyers and sellers, since price and quantity both change
Only buyers, because the price changed
Only sellers, because they set the price
Nobody, because the market returns to the old point
questions.explanation: The new crossing point sits at a different price *and* a different quantity, so both sides are affected. Reading only the price change is the commonest mistake with these diagrams.

questions.stem: A tariff is placed on imported steel. What does the diagram show happening?
options: Neither curve moves
Supply shifts left: price rises, quantity falls
Supply shifts right: price falls, quantity rises
Demand shifts left
questions.explanation: A tariff raises the cost of bringing steel in, so less is supplied at every price. Supply shifts left, price rises and quantity falls — which is the cost of protection that the policy's supporters rarely mention.

questions.stem: After a tariff is placed on imported steel, who bears the effect shown?
options: Both buyers and sellers, since price and quantity both change
Only buyers, because the price changed
Only sellers, because they set the price
Nobody, because the market returns to the old point
questions.explanation: The new crossing point sits at a different price *and* a different quantity, so both sides are affected. Reading only the price change is the commonest mistake with these diagrams.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a minimum price set above equilibrium. What does the orange gap show?
options: The total revenue in the market
The size of the government subsidy
A surplus: sellers offer more than buyers will take
A shortage: buyers want more than sellers offer
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and the difference is a surplus. A minimum wage is the example most students meet: the surplus is unemployment.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a maximum price set below equilibrium. What does the orange gap show?
options: The tax collected by government
A shortage: buyers want more than sellers offer
A surplus: sellers offer more than buyers will take
The profit made by sellers
questions.explanation: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and the difference is a shortage. Rent controls are the standard example, and queues or waiting lists are what the shortage looks like in practice.

questions.stem: Why does a price floor only have an effect when it is set above equilibrium?
options: Because supply is fixed in the short run
Because buyers ignore prices set by government
Below equilibrium the market price is already legal, so nothing binds
Floors are always set above equilibrium by law
questions.explanation: A floor beneath the market price permits a price nobody wanted to charge anyway, so it changes nothing. Only a binding control — a floor above or a ceiling below — moves the market off equilibrium.

questions.stem: A minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage. What does the diagram predict?
options: Nothing changes in the labour market
More people want jobs than employers will hire
Employers hire more workers than before
The wage falls back to equilibrium
questions.explanation: The surplus of labour is unemployment: at the higher wage more people offer to work and fewer are hired. Economists disagree about the size of this effect in practice, but the diagram is what the argument is about.

questions.stem: In the circular flow model, what do households provide to firms?
options: Labour and other resources
Goods and services
Taxes only
Interest rates
questions.explanation: Households supply labour, land and capital, and firms pay wages, rent and profit in return. The two flows run in opposite directions, which is what makes the model a circle.

questions.stem: In the circular flow model, what flows from firms to households?
options: Only imports
Interest rates set by the RBA
Goods and services, and income for the resources supplied
Only taxes
questions.explanation: Firms send goods and services one way and wages and income the other. Money flows one way round the circle and real things flow the other.

questions.stem: Why is the circular flow described as a model rather than a description?
options: It shows what should happen rather than what does
It simplifies deliberately, leaving out government, banks and trade
It has never been tested with real data
It applies only to small economies
questions.explanation: The two-sector version is the simplest form. Fuller versions add government, the financial sector and overseas — each one a further leakage and injection into the same circle.

questions.stem: In the circular flow, what happens if households save more of their income?
options: The flow of resources stops entirely
Nothing, because saving is not part of the model
Less flows back to firms as spending, so the circle slows
Firms automatically produce more
questions.explanation: Saving is a leakage: income that does not return as spending. Investment is the matching injection, and whether the two balance is much of what macroeconomic policy is about.

questions.stem: The chart plots the unemployment rate over time. What does it show?
options: Unemployment is falling
The indicator has not changed
The chart shows prices rather than a rate
Unemployment is rising
questions.explanation: Rising unemployment usually signals a slowing economy. It is a lagging indicator: firms cut hours before they cut jobs, so it turns after the downturn has already begun.

questions.stem: The chart plots the inflation rate over time. What does it show?
options: Inflation is rising
Inflation is falling
The indicator has not changed
The chart shows prices rather than a rate
questions.explanation: Rising inflation means prices are climbing faster than before. The RBA's target band is 2 to 3 per cent on average over time, and sustained readings above it usually bring interest rate rises.

questions.stem: The chart plots the economic growth over time. What does it show?
options: The indicator has not changed
The chart shows prices rather than a rate
Growth is slowing
Growth is accelerating
questions.explanation: Falling growth means output is still rising but more slowly. Two consecutive quarters of negative growth is the common definition of a recession, which is a further step down from this.

questions.stem: Inflation is rising as the chart shows. What is the RBA most likely to do?
options: Cut the cash rate to encourage spending
Raise government spending
Reduce income tax
Raise the cash rate to slow spending
questions.explanation: Monetary policy is the RBA's tool and the cash rate is its lever. Raising it makes borrowing dearer and saving more attractive, cooling demand. Government spending and tax are fiscal policy, which is the Treasurer's.

questions.stem: Unemployment is rising as the chart shows. Which response is fiscal policy?
options: Banks lower their lending standards
The government increases spending on infrastructure
The RBA cuts the cash rate
The RBA buys government bonds
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxation; monetary policy is the RBA's cash rate. Telling the two apart is worth more marks than any other distinction in this topic.
